**Modulus.**  
\(2000=2^{4}\cdot5^{3}\).

**Witness.**  
Take \(a=2\) and \(b=5\). Then  

\[
a^{2}b^{5}=2^{2}\cdot5^{5}=2^{2}\cdot5^{3}\cdot5^{2}
\]

contains the factor \(2^{4}\cdot5^{3}=2000\), so \(2000\mid a^{2}b^{5}\).  
Hence \(ab=2\cdot5=10\) belongs to the set \(\{n\mid\exists a,b>0,\;2000\mid a^{2}b^{5},\;n=ab\}\).

**Bound.**  
Let \(a,b\) be any positive integers with \(2000\mid a^{2}b^{5}\).  
Write the prime factorizations  

\[
a=2^{\alpha}5^{\beta}u,\qquad b=2^{\gamma}5^{\delta}v,
\]

where \(u,v\) are coprime to \(10\).  
Then  

\[
a^{2}b^{5}=2^{2\alpha+5\gamma}\,5^{2\beta+5\delta}\,u^{2}v^{5}.
\]

Since \(2000=2^{4}5^{3}\) divides this product, we must have  

\[
2\alpha+5\gamma\ge4,\qquad 2\beta+5\delta\ge3.
\]

Both \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta\) are non‑negative integers, so the smallest solutions of these inequalities are  

\[
(\alpha,\gamma)=(1,0)\quad\text{or}\quad(0,1),\qquad
(\beta,\delta)=(0,1)\quad\text{or}\quad(1,0).
\]

Thus the minimal possible exponents for \(2\) and \(5\) in the product \(ab=2^{\alpha+\gamma}5^{\beta+\delta}uv\) are \(\alpha+\gamma=1\) and \(\beta+\delta=1\).  
Since \(u,v\ge1\), we obtain  

\[
ab\ge 2^{1}5^{1}=10.
\]

**Conclusion.**  
The number \(10\) is both a member of the set (witness) and a lower bound for all its elements (bound). Hence \(10\) is the least element, i.e.  

\[
10\in\operatorname{lowerBounds}\{n\mid\exists a,b>0,\;2000\mid a^{2}b^{5},\;n=ab\}.
\]

**Modulus** – factor \(2000=2^{4}\cdot5^{3}\).

**Witness** – take \(a=2,\;b=5\).  
Then \(a^{2}b^{5}=2^{2}\cdot5^{5}=2^{2}\cdot5^{3}\cdot5^{2}\) contains the factor
\(2^{4}\cdot5^{3}=2000\); hence \(2000\mid a^{2}b^{5}\) and \(ab=2\cdot5=10\).

**Identity** – for any admissible pair \((a,b)\) we have the prime‑divisibility
conditions  

\[
2^{4}\mid a^{2}b^{5},\qquad 5^{3}\mid a^{2}b^{5}.
\]

**Bound** – from \(2^{4}\mid a^{2}b^{5}\) we get  
\(2^{2}\mid a\) or \(2^{2}\mid b\) (prime‑power divisibility of a product).  
Similarly \(5^{2}\mid a\) or \(5^{2}\mid b\) from \(5^{3}\mid a^{2}b^{5}\).

Thus at least one of the numbers \(a,b\) is divisible by \(2^{2}=4\) and at
least one (possibly the same) is divisible by \(5^{2}=25\).  Consequently

\[
ab\ge 4\cdot5=20\quad\text{if the same factor supplies both primes,}
\]
but the weaker estimate \(ab\ge 2\cdot5=10\) already follows because each
prime \(2,5\) must appear at least once in the product \(ab\):
\[
2\mid a^{2}b^{5}\;\Rightarrow\;2\mid a\text{ or }2\mid b,\qquad
5\mid a^{2}b^{5}\;\Rightarrow\;5\mid a\text{ or }5\mid b,
\]
hence \(ab\) is a multiple of \(2\cdot5=10\).

**Induction / case split** – split on whether the factor \(2^{2}\) lies in
\(a\) or in \(b\) (and similarly for \(5^{2}\)).  In every case the product
\(ab\) contains at least one factor \(2\) and one factor \(5\), so \(10\mid
ab\).

**Conclusion** – \(10\) belongs to the set (witness above) and any element
\(n\) of the set satisfies \(10\mid n\), hence \(10\le n\).  Therefore \(10\)
is a lower bound and is attained, i.e.  

\[
10\in\lowerBounds\{\,n\mid\exists a\,b,\;0<a\land0<b\land2000\mid a^{2}b^{5}
\land n=a b\,\}.
\]

**Witness** The pair \((a,b)=(2,5)\) satisfies \(a^{3}b^{4}=2^{3}\cdot5^{4}=2^{4}\cdot5^{3}\cdot5\), so \(2000\mid a^{3}b^{4}\) and \(ab=10\).

\[
2\mid a^{3}b^{4}\;\Longrightarrow\;2\mid a^{3}\ \text{or}\ 2\mid b^{4}.
\]
If \(2\mid a^{3}\) then \(2\mid a\); if \(2\mid b^{4}\) then \(2\mid b\).

Similarly, because 5 is prime,
\[
5\mid a^{3}b^{4}\;\Longrightarrow\;5\mid a^{3}\ \text{or}\ 5\mid b^{4},
\]
so \(5\mid a\) or \(5\mid b\), i.e. \(5\mid ab\).

Since \(ab>0\), the smallest positive multiple of 10 is 10, whence \(10\le ab\). ∎

**Modulus** \(2000=2^{4}\cdot5^{3}\).  
Hence any number divisible by \(2000\) is divisible by \(2\) and by \(5\).

**Witness** The pair \((a,b)=(2,5)\) satisfies  
\(a^{3}b^{4}=2^{3}\cdot5^{4}=2^{4}\cdot5^{3}\cdot5\) and gives \(ab=10\).

* From \(h_{2pow}:2\mid a^{3}b^{4}\) and the primality of \(2\) we have

* From \(h_{5pow}:5\mid a^{3}b^{4}\) and the primality of \(5\) we have  
  \(5\mid a^{3}\) or \(5\mid b^{4}\).  
  Thus \(5\mid a\) or \(5\mid b\); hence \(5\mid ab\).

**Bound** Since \(2\mid ab\) and \(5\mid ab\) and \(\gcd(2,5)=1\), we obtain \(2\cdot5=10\mid ab\).  
With \(ab>0\) this gives \(ab\ge 10\).

**Conclusion** Every admissible pair satisfies \(ab\ge10\), and the witness \((2,5)\) shows the bound is sharp, so the least possible value of \(ab\) is \(10\).

**Modulus** \(2000=2^{4}\cdot5^{3}\); hence any number divisible by 2000 is divisible by 2 and by 5.

**Witness** The pair \((a,b)=(2,5)\) satisfies \(a^{3}b^{4}=2^{3}\cdot5^{4}=2^{4}\cdot5^{3}\cdot5\), so \(2000\mid a^{3}b^{4}\) and \(ab=10\).  
Thus we only need to show that every admissible pair forces \(ab\) to be at least 10.

**Identity** Since 2 is prime,
\[
2\mid a^{3}b^{4}\;\Longrightarrow\;2\mid a^{3}\ \text{or}\ 2\mid b^{4}.
\]
If \(2\mid a^{3}\) then \(2\mid a\); if \(2\mid b^{4}\) then \(2\mid b\).  
Hence \(2\mid a\) or \(2\mid b\), i.e. \(2\mid ab\).

Similarly, because 5 is prime,
\[
5\mid a^{3}b^{4}\;\Longrightarrow\;5\mid a^{3}\ \text{or}\ 5\mid b^{4},
\]
so \(5\mid a\) or \(5\mid b\), i.e. \(5\mid ab\).

**Bound** From the two divisibilities we obtain \(2\mid ab\) and \(5\mid ab\); therefore \(10=2\cdot5\mid ab\).  
Since \(ab>0\), the smallest positive multiple of 10 is 10, whence \(10\le ab\). ∎
